frames.narration: A user taps 'send code'. The app calls the send API with the phone number and an idempotency key. The fraud guard checks the limits for this number and that the destination range has a healthy verification rate, and lets it through.
The OTP service draws a six-digit code from a secure random generator. It keeps only a salted hash, with an expiry of 5 minutes and a count of 0 of 5 attempts.

The API saves a message record in the state 'queued' and puts its id on the queue. The app gets the message id at once. If it retried with the same key, it would get this same id back and nothing else would be queued.

A worker takes the message to the router. Provider A is cheaper, but its circuit breaker is open after repeated failures, so the router skips it and chooses provider B, the cheapest healthy route for this country.
Provider B accepts the message and returns its own reference. The router records it, and the message moves to 'sent'.

The carrier delivers the SMS and the code appears on the handset, 3 seconds after the tap. The carrier then sends a signed delivery receipt, which moves the record to 'delivered' and feeds B's quality figures.

The user types the code. The OTP service hashes the guess, compares it in constant time, finds it correct on attempt 1 of 5 within the 5 minutes, and marks the code used. The same code would now be refused.
The successful check counts as a verified send for this destination range. The fraud guard uses these counts: a range with many sends and almost no verifications would be blocked.
